articles.title: I built a platform because getting honest feedback on your project shouldn't be this hard
articles.excerpt: You spend weeks building something. You finally launch it. Then... silence. Your friends say it's great. People might like your post. But nobody tells you what actually needs improvement. That's the p…
articles.body: You spend weeks building something. You finally launch it. Then... silence. Your friends say it's great. People might like your post. But nobody tells you what actually needs improvement. That's the problem I wanted to solve. The problem As developers and indie makers, we spend so much time building products, but getting useful feedback is surprisingly difficult. You don't know what users actually think. Friends are often too nice to criticize your work. Posting on social media doesn't guarantee meaningful feedback. You need honest opinions, not just likes. Sometimes, one honest answer is more valuable than a hundred likes. What I'm building I'm building Critique — an open-source platform where makers share their projects, ask one focused question, and get feedback from real people.
articles.author: Dinesh Bista

articles.title: How 1Password was breached through one GitHub account
articles.excerpt: 1Password disclosed on November 25 that an attacker got into some of its backend systems and copied account records for a subset of its customers. Names and sign-in email addresses were in that data.…
articles.body: 1Password disclosed on November 25 that an attacker got into some of its backend systems and copied account records for a subset of its customers. Names and sign-in email addresses were in that data. Vault contents were not, and 1Password says they were never reachable. The way in was a single employee's corporate GitHub account. From there the attacker read private source code, got into CI/CD and pushed code to production. That is a short path from one login to the backend of a password manager, and it is the part every software team should read twice. Timeline of the 1Password breach Here is the timeline from 1Password's disclosure, as covered by 9to5Mac: November 19, 2026. 1Password starts investigating signs that an attacker had access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

articles.title: Prompt caching and marketplace pricing: where the discount really lands
articles.excerpt: Prompt caching and marketplace pricing: where the discount really lands Published 2026-11-28 · LONG AI Engineering Notes The most common budgeting mistake I see with prompt caching is treating it as a…
articles.body: Prompt caching and marketplace pricing: where the discount really lands Published 2026-11-28 · LONG AI Engineering Notes The most common budgeting mistake I see with prompt caching is treating it as a second discount stacked on top of a marketplace discount. People reason: "I get 50% off official price here, and caching saves me 90% of input tokens, so my input cost is 5% of official." That arithmetic never holds, and the reason is not greed — it is that the two discounts multiply different things. Caching discounts the cacheable portion of input. A marketplace discount discounts the unit price of the whole request . Apply them in the wrong order, or apply them to the wrong token count, and the number you put in your budget is fiction. 1.

articles.excerpt: A few weeks after part 1 went out, someone opened an issue on DotMorph asking for one thing: drag an audio file onto the wheel and get its text back, as a file or straight to the clipboard. It was a g…
articles.body: A few weeks after part 1 went out, someone opened an issue on DotMorph asking for one thing: drag an audio file onto the wheel and get its text back, as a file or straight to the clipboard. It was a good request, and it changed how I thought about the app. Until then DotMorph converted formats : PNG to WebP, MOV to MP4. A transcript isn't another format of the same audio. It's what the audio says . The same goes for a screenshot of an error message, or a scanned invoice. So 2.2 teaches DotMorph to listen and to read, without breaking the rule that nothing leaves your machine. Why whisper.cpp, and not "pip install whisper" OpenAI's Whisper is the obvious model.

articles.title: GitHub Action to scan your deployed AI-built app on every deploy (proofforge.live)
articles.excerpt: Most AI-built apps get checked once, by hand, right before launch. Then the next deploy changes a header, a CORS rule or a storage policy, and nobody looks again. A scan that runs on every deploy catc…
articles.body: Most AI-built apps get checked once, by hand, right before launch. Then the next deploy changes a header, a CORS rule or a storage policy, and nobody looks again. A scan that runs on every deploy catches that drift. I'm part of the ProofForge team, and we published a GitHub Action that does this from the outside. It is listed in the GitHub Marketplace: ProofForge outside security check . The source is at proofforge-live/scan-action . What it does It runs ProofForge's free, read-only outside scan against a live URL you own. It looks at what a stranger can see: public pages, headers, exposed files, and client-side bundles. It never signs in, so it cannot see behind your login. Treat the grade as an outside view, not a full audit.

articles.title: Every Last Grain: a browser game where the mechanic is patience
articles.excerpt: Browser games usually ask for a download, an account or a store page. Every Last Grain asks for one thing: patience with a shovel. The premise is small. You work the Lot Edge, a square of desert, and…
articles.body: Browser games usually ask for a download, an account or a store page. Every Last Grain asks for one thing: patience with a shovel. The premise is small. You work the Lot Edge, a square of desert, and you dig it by the kilo. Fourteen finds are buried in the grid, and nothing tells you where they are except the ground itself: the tone of the dirt, the shape of the pile, the way a patch settles after you lift it. That is the whole game, and it is more interesting than it sounds. Digging by the kilo means every swing costs something, so you stop treating the field as a list of places to click and start treating it as material to read. Most browser games fail at exactly this point: they hand you a map and call it a mechanic. What the design gets right No download in the way.

articles.title: 12 grains of dust found high in Earth's atmosphere reveal secrets of water at the edge of the solar system
articles.excerpt: Grains of dust found floating in Earth's stratosphere hold the secrets of a special kind of 'heavy' water that seems to be abundant in the outer solar system.
articles.body: A dozen grains of dust that have wandered in from the distant Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune were found floating in Earth's stratosphere. And it turns out they hold the secrets of a special kind of 'heavy' water that seems to be surprisingly abundant in the outer solar system. When analyzed by a team of scientists the 12 dust grains, which were captured by NASA's stratospheric ER-2 research aircraft, show signs of having interacted with a form of water that contains heavy oxygen isotopes. This is important because to better understand how the planets formed, scientists are seeking to understand how various materials were distributed around the early solar system 4.5 billion years ago.

articles.body: A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.
